name: Interview finance, set 2
description: Finance questions of the kind asked in online assessments and first rounds: present values, yields, forward arbitrage, margin, covered calls, butterflies, option bounds, gamma, digitals, trees, book prices, impact, value at risk and baskets. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: You will receive £500 at the end of each of the next three years. The discount rate is 8% a year.
items.question: What is the present value, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: £1,288.55: each £500 discounted for its own year.
widget.label: Present value in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount each payment by 1.08 to the power of its year, then add.

byKey.not-discounted: You added the payments without discounting. Money paid later is worth less today.
byKey.all-three-years: You discounted every payment for three years. The first is paid after one year and the second after two.

explain.text: Discount each payment by its own year: $500/1.08 + 500/1.08^2 + 500/1.08^3$. Those are 462.96, 428.67 and 396.92. They sum to £1,288.55.

items.prose: A zero-coupon bond maturing in five years costs 78.35 now and repays 100.
items.question: What is its annual yield, in per cent to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the yearly growth factor that turns 78.35 into 100 over five years.

byKey.simple-interest: You used simple interest, the 21.65 gain over 78.35 spread over five years. A zero-coupon yield compounds each year.
byKey.gain-over-five: You divided the gain of 21.65 by 5. Compare the gain with the price paid, and compound it.

explain.text: The yield y solves $78.35(1 + y)^5 = 100$. Since $1.05^5 = 1.27628$ and $100/78.35 = 1.27632$, the growth factor is 1.05 to four places. So the yield is about 5.00%.

items.prose: A share costs £200 and pays a £4 dividend at the end of the year. You can borrow and lend at 3% simple for the year. A one-year forward on the share is quoted at £205.
items.question: How much does the arbitrage make per share at delivery, in pounds?

widget.accept: £3: the quote is £3 above the fair £202.
widget.label: Profit in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the fair forward with the dividend, then trade against the quote.

byKey.no-dividend: You left out the dividend, so fair value looked like £206. Holding the share earns the £4, so fair is £202.
byKey.dividend-twice: You took the dividend off twice. Fair value is 206 less 4, which is £202.

explain.text: Fair value is the cost of carry less the dividend: $200 \times 1.03 - 4 = 202$ pounds. The quote is £3 rich, so sell the forward, borrow £200 and buy the share. At delivery the £205 and the £4 dividend repay the £206 you owe, leaving £3.

items.prose: You are long 10 index futures, each worth £50 per index point. The index falls from 4,000 to 3,960 in a day.
items.question: What is your loss on the day, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the points lost by the value of a point and by the number of contracts.

byKey.one-contract: You gave the loss on one contract. You hold 10 of them.
byKey.points-times-contracts: You multiplied the 40 points by the 10 contracts and stopped. Each point is worth £50 a contract.

explain.text: The index fell $4{,}000 - 3{,}960 = 40$ points. Each contract loses £50 a point, so one contract loses £2,000. Ten contracts lose $10 \times 2{,}000 = 20{,}000$ pounds, paid from your margin.

items.prose: You buy a share at £40 and sell a call on it struck at £45 for £2. At expiry the share is at £50.
items.question: What is your profit, in pounds?

widget.accept: £7: 5 on the share up to the strike, plus the £2 premium.
widget.label: Profit in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The call caps what you get for the share; add the premium you kept.

byKey.no-cap: You kept the share's whole rise to £50. The call you sold is exercised, so you deliver the share at £45.
byKey.no-premium: You left out the £2 premium. You received it when you sold the call.

explain.text: The share is called away at £45, a gain of $45 - 40 = 5$ pounds. You also keep the £2 premium. So the profit is $5 + 2 = 7$ pounds, however high the share goes.

items.prose: Calls struck at 90, 100 and 110 cost £12.50, £6.00 and £2.50. You buy one 90 call, sell two 100 calls and buy one 110 call.
items.question: What is the largest profit at expiry, in pounds?

widget.accept: £7: a payoff of 10 at 100 less the £3 cost.
widget.label: Largest profit in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the net cost, then the payoff with the share at the middle strike.

byKey.ignored-cost: You gave the largest payoff, 10, and left out the £3 the butterfly costs.
byKey.gave-cost: You gave the net cost of the butterfly. The question asks for the payoff less that cost.

explain.text: The butterfly costs $12.50 - 2 \times 6.00 + 2.50 = 3$ pounds. Its payoff peaks at 10 with the share at 100. So the largest profit is $10 - 3 = 7$ pounds.

items.prose: A share is at £100, the interest rate is zero and there are no dividends. A European call on it struck at £95 trades at £4.50.
items.question: You buy the call and short the share. What is the smallest profit this locks in, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: £0.50: the floor of £5 less the £4.50 price.
widget.label: Smallest profit in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the call's lower bound with zero rate, then compare it with the price.

byKey.gave-floor: You gave the lower bound, 100 less 95. The call costs £4.50, so the locked-in profit is the gap below that bound.
byKey.gave-price: You gave the call's price. The profit is how far that price sits under its floor of £5.

explain.text: With zero rate a call is worth at least $100 - 95 = 5$ pounds. Buy it for £4.50 and short the share for £100, which leaves £95.50 in hand. At expiry you buy back the share for at most £95, so you keep at least $95.50 - 95 = 0.50$ pounds.

items.prose: You hold a delta-hedged long option with gamma 0.04. It loses £0.045 a day to theta.
items.question: What daily share move breaks even, in pounds to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the gamma gain from a move equal to the day's theta.

byKey.no-half: You left out the half in the gamma term, so you solved 0.04 times the move squared equals 0.045. The gain is half of gamma times the move squared.
byKey.no-root: You stopped at the squared move, 2.25. Take its square root.

explain.text: A hedged option gains $\tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma\,dS^2$ from a move and loses theta. Break even when $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.04 \times dS^2 = 0.045$, so the squared move is 2.25. The move is $\sqrt{2.25} = 1.5$ pounds.

items.prose: A share is at £50. A digital call pays £1 at expiry if the share ends above £50. Volatility is 30% a year, the option has three months to run and the interest rate is zero.
items.question: What is the digital call worth, in pounds to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With zero rate a digital call is worth the risk-neutral chance of finishing above the strike.

byKey.one-half: You took the chance of ending above the strike as one half. The share's risk-neutral median sits below today's price, so the chance is a little less.
byKey.used-d1: You used $N(d_1)$, the call's delta. The digital pays on the risk-neutral chance $N(d_2)$.

explain.text: A digital call is worth $N(d_2)$ when the rate is zero. Here $d_2 = -\sigma\sqrt{T}/2$, which is $-0.3 \times 0.5/2 = -0.075$. So the price is $N(-0.075) \approx 0.4701$ pounds.

items.prose: A share is at £40. At each of two steps it is multiplied by 1.25 or by 0.8, and the interest rate is zero.
items.question: What is a two-step European call struck at £40 worth, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the risk-neutral up chance, then weight the top payoff by the chance of two ups.

byKey.even-chances: You used even chances of up and down. The risk-neutral up chance is 4/9, set so the share's expected price stays 40.
byKey.q-once: You weighted 22.50 by q once. Reaching the top node takes two up moves, so weight it by q squared.

explain.text: The up chance is $q = (1 - 0.8)/(1.25 - 0.8) = 4/9$. Only two ups pay, with the share at 62.50 and the call worth 22.50. The price is $(4/9)^2 \times 22.5 = 40/9 \approx 4.44$ pounds.

items.prose: The book shows 900 shares bid at 99.98 and 100 shares offered at 100.02.
items.question: Weighting each price by the size on the other side, what is the size-weighted mid, to 3 decimal places?

widget.accept: 100.016: the bid weighted by 100 and the ask by 900.
widget.label: Weighted mid

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the bid by the ask size and the ask by the bid size. Then divide by the total size.

byKey.own-side: You weighted each price by its own size. The question weights it by the size on the other side.
byKey.plain-mid: You gave the plain mid. The sizes are lopsided, so the weighted mid moves towards the ask.

explain.text: Weight the bid by the ask size and the ask by the bid size: $(99.98 \times 100 + 100.02 \times 900)/1{,}000$. That is $(9{,}998 + 90{,}018)/1{,}000 = 100.016$. The heavy bid suggests the next trade is more likely at the ask.

items.prose: Under a square-root impact model, an order for 4% of daily volume costs 40 basis points.
items.question: What does an order for 16% of daily volume cost, in basis points?

widget.accept: 80: twice the cost for four times the size.
widget.label: Cost in basis points

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the cost by the square root of the change in size.

byKey.linear: You scaled the cost in line with size. Under a square-root model, four times the size costs twice as much.
byKey.no-change: You kept the cost the same. A larger order moves the price further, so it costs more per share.

explain.text: Impact grows with the square root of the order's share of volume. Four times the size is $\sqrt{4} = 2$ times the cost. So the cost is $40 \times 2 = 80$ basis points.

items.prose: As a market maker you trade 1,000 shares and earn a half-spread of 1p on each. After each trade the price moves 0.4p against you on average.
items.question: What is your net result, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the move away from the half-spread on each share.

byKey.ignored-move: You kept the whole half-spread. The move against you costs 0.4p a share.
byKey.added-move: You added the move to the spread. It goes against you, so it comes off.

explain.text: Each share earns 1p of spread and loses 0.4p to the move, so it nets 0.6p. Over 1,000 shares that is 600p. That is £6.

items.prose: Two desks each have a one-day value at risk of £1m. Their P&L is normal with mean zero, and the correlation between the desks is 0.5.
items.question: What is their combined value at risk, in £ millions to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the two figures as you would two standard deviations.

byKey.added: You added the two figures. That holds only at correlation 1; at 0.5 the desks partly offset.
byKey.no-correlation: You combined them as if independent, the root of 2. The correlation term adds $2 \times 0.5 = 1$ under the root.

explain.text: For normal P&L with zero mean, value at risk scales like a standard deviation. So the combined figure is $\sqrt{1 + 1 + 2 \times 0.5} = \sqrt{3}$ in £ millions. That is about £1.732m, less than the £2m sum.

items.prose: Two shares each trade at £100 with the same volatility, and the rate is zero. You compare a call on a basket of half of each share with half a call on each share. All are struck at £100 with one year to run.
items.question: Which costs more?

options.text: The two half calls, unless the shares move exactly together.
The basket call, as it is written on two shares at once.
options.why: You counted the basket as more exposure. Its two halves partly offset each other, so it is less volatile and worth less.

options.text: They always cost the same, since the payoffs share a strike.
options.why: You equated the payoffs. A basket at the strike can hide one share far above it, which a separate call would pay on.

options.text: It depends only on the interest rate, not on correlation.
options.why: You looked to the rate. The gap comes from correlation: the lower it is, the more the basket's moves cancel.

feedback.correct: Correct. The separate calls cost more unless the shares move as one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the payoffs path by path: can the basket call ever pay more?

explain.text: A call's payoff is convex, so two half calls always pay at least what the basket call pays. They match only when the shares move as one. At vol 25% and correlation 0.3, the half calls cost £9.95 and the basket call about £8.05.
